title: DNS TXT Beaconing Periodicity
summary: DNS TXT beaconing periodicity detection identifies recurring queries for TXT records that follow a regular timing pattern toward the same parent domain or a small set of parent domains, which is the characteristic signature of command and control or data transfer tunnelled through the Domain Name System. The behaviour matters because DNS is almost universally permitted outbound, is rarely inspected beyond basic reputation filtering, and is handled by infrastructure that neither authenticates the requester nor understands the payload carried in record data, so an operator can both task an implant and receive results without ever opening a conventional network connection to an unfamiliar address. The telemetry required is DNS query and response logging from recursive resolvers, the endpoint DNS client cache or sensor, or passive network capture of DNS traffic, retaining the queried name, record type, response size, response code and the requesting host, together with a source of timing aggregation so periodicity and jitter can be measured rather than inferred. The signal survives common evasion because tunnelling still requires a sustained exchange of queries and answers; even an implant that introduces jitter must remain within the beacon interval the operator needs for practical interactivity, and adding jitter reduces but does not eliminate measurable regularity in the same destination. Domain fronting, long label payloads and rapid parent-domain rotation do change the observable distribution, but rotation itself produces an anomalous pattern of newly registered parents on the resolver. The detection breaks down in practice because many benign applications resolve on fixed schedules: telemetry agents, update checkers, endpoint management clients and messaging clients all poll on intervals. Shared resolvers also mask which internal host issued a query when logging is aggregated, and encrypted DNS removes query visibility entirely at the network layer. Practical reliability comes from combining timing regularity with query characteristics such as TXT record focus, unusually long or high-entropy labels, high unique-subdomain counts per parent, and rare-parent-domain age, and from accepting that encrypted DNS requires endpoint-side logging to remain detectable.
objectives: Explain why DNS is a durable command and control channel and which record types are most abused for bidirectional exchange.
Measure beacon periodicity and jitter from resolver logs and choose statistics that tolerate normal scheduling drift.
Combine timing regularity with label entropy, unique subdomain count and parent domain age to reduce false positives.
Identify which hosts in the estate bypass local resolver logging through encrypted DNS and describe the compensating control.
Correlate DNS anomalies with endpoint process telemetry to attribute queries to a specific binary and parent.
Rank a suspected tunnelling channel against other active incidents using data volume, target asset criticality and confidence.

dataSources: Recursive DNS resolver query logs containing queried name, record type, response code and requesting client address
Endpoint DNS client telemetry associating each query with the process that issued it
Passive network capture of DNS requests and responses with response length and timing
Domain registration and reputation enrichment providing parent domain age, registrar and hosting classification
Proxy and firewall logs showing whether the same host used other egress channels in the same window
logic: Group DNS queries by requesting host and parent domain, restrict attention to record types that carry data such as TXT, and compute whether successive queries to the same parent arrive at a stable interval with low variance relative to the host's normal traffic. Raise an alert when periodicity is combined with data-bearing record types, unusually long or random-looking labels, a high count of distinct subdomains under one parent, or a parent domain that is recently registered or heavily queried from a single host. Then attribute the queries to a process using endpoint telemetry so the responder knows whether the source is a known agent or an unexplained binary, and cross-check for other egress activity in the same window before deciding severity.
pseudoQuery:
title: Periodic DNS TXT Queries To A Single Parent Domain
id: det-dns-txt-beaconing
status: training
logsource:
  category: dns_query
detection:
  txt_queries:
    RecordType: TXT
  label_characteristics:
    QueryName|re: '^[A-Za-z0-9+/=_-]{20,}\\.'
  periodicity:
    condition: stdev(query_interval) < 5s and count() by Hostname, ParentDomain > 30 within 1h
  high_diversity:
    condition: count(distinct QueryName) by Hostname, ParentDomain > 50 within 1h
  condition: txt_queries and periodicity and (label_characteristics or high_diversity)
fields:
  - Hostname
  - QueryName
  - RecordType
  - QueryLength
  - ResponseCode
level: high
falsePositives: Endpoint management, patching and telemetry agents that poll vendor services on a fixed schedule
Anti-abuse and reputation services that issue repeated lookups to the same provider as part of normal operation
Content filtering and secure web gateways that validate domains through their own resolver pipeline
Application health checks and service discovery that resolve infrastructure names at a constant interval
Email security platforms performing repeated sender domain and record validation
tuningNotes: Build a per-host periodic-query baseline and allow-list the destination parents used by signed agents, but exclude only the specific host-and-parent pair rather than the host entirely, so a compromised workstation running legitimate agents can still generate an alert for a different parent. Relax the variance threshold in environments where schedulers drift, and compensate by tightening the label entropy and subdomain diversity conditions, which are harder for legitimate software to satisfy accidentally. Keep TXT as a strong weighting factor rather than a hard requirement, because tunnelling also occurs over other record types, and review the rule monthly against the current top parent domains so that newly adopted cloud services do not produce sustained noise. Where encrypted DNS is deployed, ensure the compensating endpoint logging source is onboarded before relying on this detection for compliance reporting.
